blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Good morning, Dr Ventress.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Good morning.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Before we continue with where I left off yesterday, I'd be grateful if we could just clarify the order in which particular events happened from the notes --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- just before we go through them and then I'll pick up from where I'd got to. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up on the screens tile 80 from the [Baby G] section 1 section.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, if you're following it on the iPads, you know how to get there, so tile 80.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a feature of the notes. They are over three pages, but tile 80 has the first two pages on and then tile 107 has pages 2 and 3 on, so there's a bit of an overlap that way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see them, Dr Ventress?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Can you see them, ladies and gentlemen? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is just to get back in our heads the order in which things happened. There's some dense detail here.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Starting on tile 80, you are called at 02.35?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You make the notes at 04.40 or you start making the notes, but you were called at 2.35 and you went from the children's ward to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I assume I was on the children's ward. I don't know definitely. I wasn't on the neonatal unit according to the notes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm not going to go through the detail of everything right now, we've been through a lot of the details, and there are some items I am going to go to, but I just want to get the order in which things happened clear.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At 2.35, you go to the neonatal unit. Once you'd been there, you had to leave because you were called away back to the maternity unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So let's go over the page then to the second page of slide 80, just to follow the sequence of where we get to.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Having left, you were then called back to the neonatal unit. And when we looked at the timings it looks like it's some time just before 3.30, maybe about 3.20.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So you're next back at 3.20. And at that point there has been a report of another desaturation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's the first desaturation.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's the first desaturation. Thank you. That's important. Thank you. That's the first desaturation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby G] is moved to room 1. Dr Brearey has been called.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And then [Baby G], having been moved to room 1, there is a further desaturation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. So this is the second desaturation. And you take the decision that it's going to be necessary to intubate [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. You do intubate [Baby G] and that's the point when you describe, as we can see in the notes halfway down, bloodstained fluid up from the trachea?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Stephen Brearey, the consultant, he then attends; that's the next thing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: To start with, things seem to be working well enough on the ventilator, we've got down here:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Good gas 30 minutes post-intubation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Then the next timing we have, three or four lines up from the bottom of the second page, is 5.30 when there's another, as it's described there, profound desaturation; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I know you're nodding, Dr Ventress. It might seem a bit laborious, but you need to say yes or no.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby G] is then taken off the ventilator that she had been on, just at the bottom of that page. Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That wasn't when the ventilator was changed.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: She's taken off that ventilator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Let's go through this as it is in the notes so we get the structure of it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To get to the next page of the notes, we have to go to slide 107, so let's go there, if you would, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we go behind that to the notes. We need to go to the second page to pick up where we were. We can see:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Recovered slowly but desat when back on ventilator."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Does that suggest she was taken off the ventilator for a short period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she was disconnected so we could use the Neopuff device.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So we've had a further desat at 5.30, then disconnected from the ventilator so the Neopuff could be used.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Recovered slowly, back on the ventilator, but then desaturated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: This is the point at which you check the flow sensor or the flow sensor is checked?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And then was the whole -- it says "whole ventilator changed".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So you switched to a different ventilator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. Next, 6.05, another desaturation, down to 40%; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It says "IPPV given". That's intermittent positive --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Pressure ventilation.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So she's off the ventilator again at that point, [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Whenever it says IPPV, that would refer to the Neopuff device.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So 6.05, profound desaturation. Off the ventilator. On to the Neopuff. And then we see the ETT removed at 6.10; that's the next thing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: When that was removed, thick secretions were found in the mouth, plus plus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And a blood clot on the end of the ETT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's the endotracheal tube. I'll come back to that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The Neopuff continues to be used; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Then this time with a mask instead of via the ETT.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Three lines below that we can see:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Dr Brearey called in urgently."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So he must have gone away but was called back; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: At this point, the NGT, the nasogastric tube, is aspirated and there was the 100ml aspirated from that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Which, to the best of your recollection, is most probably going to be air because if it was anything other than that you'd have said so?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And then we come to 6.15. [Baby G] is re-intubated, this time with a slightly larger 3.5 endotracheal tube?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Which you described as a "tight fit through the cords"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You see bloodstained fluid in the oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Suction takes place, but from this point on, so far as the ventilation is concerned, things seem to settle; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, as far as I've documented there, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: As far as it goes, all right. I just wanted to go back through that so we had the stages that we go through with what we have in the notes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to go back to the detail now to go through some of what we have looked at, you were called back for the second time a little bit before 3.30 because of a desaturation that had taken place, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put back up tile 80, just in case we want to follow this as I go through the questions now. We're on page 2 of that tile.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So you've been called back for that. And then the second desaturation happened when you were there, didn't it, so far as you can recall?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It was as a result of that that you decided it was necessary to intubate, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We got to this point yesterday, so I can pick it up from here. You'd seen, as you described in the notes, bloodstained fluid, but not fresh blood or any active bleed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... I can't say if it was fresh blood because fresh blood would just mean bright red. So it's likely to be fresh but a small amount. So if -- I said bloodstained fluid so it wasn't pure blood.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You've described it as bloodstained fluid, so fluid with bits of blood in it that would sound like?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It doesn't suggest here you identify any active bleed or fresh blood being produced from any source in the tissue, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you didn't see that, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Just moving down to the bottom of that page, let's move forwards now to approximately 5.30. Towards the bottom of that page. By this point, [Baby G] has been on the ventilator for about 30 minutes and things have been reasonably stable; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think she was intubated soon after 3.30, wasn't she, so more like 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right, 2 hours stable. Just looking up from approximately 5.30, six lines up, we've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Good gas 30 minutes post-intubation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Good gas 30 minutes post-intubation. Large leak noted on ETT but good air entry."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: "Vitamin K given."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's to improve the clotting process, isn't it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- in case there's a bleed? And:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Approximately 5.30, had a further profound desaturation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then that's the period when we go into trying to work out what it is that's happening with the ventilators or with the flow; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's what happens. When there was a problem with the ventilator, do you recall, did it alarm or was it just something that you noticed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... I don't recall that there was a problem, that there was -- there would have been alarms that her oxygen levels and heart rate had dropped from the monitor, but I don't know if the ventilator was alarming as well.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Sorry? Can I just be clear about that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We're talking about alarms. Can we just clarify? If the patient desaturates, an alarm goes off?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's on the monitor measuring the saturation levels?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, the heart rate, the saturation, the breathing rate are all on the monitor. If any of those go outside the set parameters then an alarm will go off.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is there an alarm on the ventilator itself?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. That would go off, for example, if say -- the flow sensor detects breath going in and out. If it stopped detecting that, the ventilator would alarm to check if something had become disconnected or -- it measures various pressures and volumes and if they're vastly outside the set limits then it can alarm for that too.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right. What alarms can you recall went off at this --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can't recall about the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Because I think it was -- I didn't know whether you were suggesting it went off or whether there were just alarms going off.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In fact I was asking whether the alarm on the ventilator went off, whether Dr Ventress has any recollection of that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You just don't know about that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I haven't documented it and I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Let's carry on then through to the end of this. If we go to slide 107 -- I apologise, ladies and gentlemen, for the coming and going, but it's having three pages over two tiles.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We get to the third page, which is on the second page of tile 107; I'm training myself to say tile instead of slide all the time. I was a slide enthusiast to begin with, but we've moved to tile I think now, my Lord. I'll try and stick with that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Tile 107, page 2. What seemed to be happening, Dr Ventress, is that when [Baby G] was taken off the ventilator and there was manual ventilation, she seemed to be all right.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But when she is put back on the ventilator there was a problem and she seemed to desaturate; that's where we get to, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's why we looked at the ventilator and the flow sensor and changed those things.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's right. In fact, you took the precaution of changing the ventilator itself, didn't you --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- to be quite clear, but even then there was a desaturation taking place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And were you there trying to work out what it was that was happening during all of this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: No criticism of that. That's what you would be doing as you want to see what is taking place.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's the standard practice, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: During all of this, a little bit below halfway down this page, is the point, some time after Dr Brearey had been called to return, that the air was aspirated from the NGT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Now, we know that [Baby G] had been receiving oxygen or receiving air manually with the Neopuff over a period of hours, hadn't she --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- on and off?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And there'd also been a period with CPAP right at the beginning, hadn't there --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, right at the beginning.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- although you didn't repeat that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What had been happening was in between each session on the ventilator, she was being given breathing assistance with the IPPV?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And in your experience, certainly, when a baby is receiving air through a breathing tube like that, air can be directed into the stomach, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So when the IPPV is being given via the ET tube then the air does not go into the stomach, but when it's given via a face mask, then the air would go into the stomach, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right. And there were times when a face mask was used, weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. After the ET tube was removed and before the ET tube was inserted for the first time.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Yes --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But there were several instances in the middle where it was used via the ET tube as well.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: As well.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But in any event --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But that wouldn't go into the stomach?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: It wouldn't then but it would when it's used via the face mask?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: In any event, when you noticed [Baby G]'s abdomen was large that struck you as something that could happen by air going into the stomach rather than the lungs?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And that's what you thought with your clinical experience at that time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That was just after she'd had a period of IPPV via the face mask.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's right. We see that. And the point is it was after that period that you noticed about her stomach being -- her abdomen being distended, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: That's it? Just so we can follow the link between those. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So IPPV with a face mask. You notice after that the abdomen appeared large and, it seems, a large quantity of air was taken from it, aspirated from the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Re-intubated after that at 06.15?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: This was with a larger, as we've just discussed, tube, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And that seemed to work better, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was less of a leak, but clinically -- yes, clinically not too much difference, I think.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: One of the things that had happened just before you did that was a clot had been removed, a blood clot from the end of the ETT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: In fact, it's quite possible is it, you tell us, if there's a clot on the end of the ETT that might have been interfering with airflow into [Baby G], mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: You have, nothing critical about this, quite properly gone through all the stages to work out what is happening, haven't you --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- including changing the ventilator --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: -- but it was when you came to withdraw the tube and check that that you saw there was a blood clot on the end of it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: So it's reasonable to take the view that will have been blocking the flow of air?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not completely but partially --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Interfering with the flow of air?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Interfering, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And the fact is that once a fresh tube was put in without a blood clot on it, [Baby G] then seemed to settle and the ventilating seemed to proceed as you'd have wanted it; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Up to the end of my note. I can't comment on what happened after that.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Absolutely. But I'm just making it quite clear, a tube without a blood clot on the end of it seemed to solve the problem; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: After that re-intubation at 6.15, or maybe during it because these things may happen together a little bit, you've described, we can see a few lines up from the X-ray sticker:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bloodstained fluid in oropharynx."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And you put:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Suction below cords but nil obtained."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Does that mean that in the -- what I might call the upper part of the throat you'd spotted some blood or bloodstained fluid?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The oropharynx is probably below where you'd see by just looking with your eyes into the mouth. I'd have seen it when I put the laryngoscope in, so it's sort of there (indicating) just below the throat.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's where you would see the entrance to the vocal cords and the food pipe, the oesophagus.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: We know there's bloodstained fluid there, but when you suction below the cords nothing comes out?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Does that suggest it's some sort of bloodstained fluid to do with the area of the cords, round about there, since there's nothing further down?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily. That's often an area where secretions and fluid will pool on a baby that's laying down, so I wouldn't be able to comment where that fluid had come from.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: But certainly no production of blood coming up from anywhere at that point that your suctioning reveals?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: And is it right, is it common or does it sometimes happen, let me put it that way, that when a baby is being intubated in that part of the throat you may get bloodstained secretions?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it's been a traumatic intubation, which does sometimes happen, especially with multiple attempts, then you can sometimes cause some trauma to the area.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: I haven't commented that I saw any obvious trauma or swelling there, which if it was a significant finding I would have commented (overspeaking) but I can't comment. I can't say 100%.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: Sorry, Dr Ventress, I interrupted you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You don't see any significant trauma around there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: There have been repeated efforts to intubate, haven't there (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There'd been one successful and this was the second one, yes.
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: All right then. So it's possible this could be something connected with the intubation process or it could be something different; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This time, yes. The first time was not connected to the --
blocks.speaker: VENTRESS

blocks.text: In a statement dated 20 November of 2018, Lara Bunni stated thus:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am currently a registrar clinical fellow in paediatric intensive care in Manchester Children's Hospital. Back in 2015 I was a senior house officer dedicated the to the neonatal unit at Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked to comment on a [Baby G] who was born on 31 May 2015 at Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Referring to medical notes, [Baby G] was born at 23.57 hours on 31 May 2015, the circumstances of which are as follows.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was working a night shift, which would have been 20.30 until 09.30 hours. I would have been covering the post-natal ward as well as the neonatal unit. My registrar at that time was Dr Vicky Nesbitt. I remember I was actually on the post-natal word reviewing a child when I heard an emergency alarm going off. I ran straight to the woman's room, which took no more than 10 seconds. That was where the alarm was coming from.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I saw [Baby G]'s mother [Mother of Baby G] sat on the toilet. [Mother of Baby G] was saying that she went to the toilet thinking she needed to go to the toilet, she felt that she'd actually had her baby in the toilet. Realising that she may have had the baby, [Mother of Baby G] said that she had pulled the emergency cord, a nurse and a healthcare assistant had arrived, but I cannot recall their names.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I asked [Mother of Baby G] to get up and move to the side of the toilet. [Baby G] was actually still attached to her mother via the umbilical cord. [Baby G] was in the water of the basin of the toilet. I scooped [Baby G] out of the toilet. At this stage the crash bleep had gone out and people started to arrive at the toilet within about 15 seconds.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I asked the staff to get me a cord clamp, a cord cutter and towels. We got the cord clamp on and cut the cord. Within 3 minutes of being born, I took her straight to the Resuscitaire. [Baby G] was not breathing. [Baby G] was the colour of blue and physically floppy. At the Resuscitaire there was myself, Dr Nesbitt and a neonatal nurse I cannot remember the name of. A hat would have been put on [Baby G] and [Baby G] would have been put in a plastic bag in order to retain [Baby G]'s heat; [Baby G] would have lost body heat whilst in the toilet water.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We then took action to stabilise [Baby G] and to get her breathing. We gave her five inflation breaths initially, which weren't effective, so we adjusted her head and gave her another five inflation breaths, which would have continued ventilation breaths as the adjustment was effective. [Baby G] was then intubated and given ventilation breaths [as read].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her heart rate was as low as 60. A 2.5-millimetre tube was inserted into [Baby G]'s throat, guided by the vocal cords. However, there was no increase in heart rate. This tube was removed. A second 2.5-millimetre tube was inserted and it was decided to leave this in as [Baby G]'s heart rate increased to 120. She seemed to be recovering.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Curosurf was then administered via the endotracheal tube to assist with the inflation and deflation of her lungs. At that point [Baby G] stabilised. She was transported via incubator to the neonatal unit intensive care nursery and placed into the NNU incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was with [Baby G] in the NNU. At that point [Baby G]'s heart rate was greater than 120. Her saturations were 90 in 80% oxygen. She was pink and well perfused.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Whilst at the NNU there was a plan to insert umbilical catheters and cannulas in order to get fluids and antibiotics into [Baby G], plus any other resuscitation medications if needed. This was all completed prior to the end of the shift with myself taking part.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Within the initial 24 to 36-hour period [Baby G] was in poor condition. She was in respiratory distress, she was intubated, she needed extra support requiring three doses of Curosurf. She had a raised CRP, which is an infection marker sign, and she was still at risk of not surviving.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Other than treating [Baby G] on her first day I did treat [Baby G] on a number of occasions. However I can't remember the dates prior to her transfer on 13 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Once things had settled down [Baby G] began feeding and growing, as we call it. However, due to her prematurity and other factors, ie being born into a toilet, she would have had blips where she would have taken a few steps back, however generally she improved.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Of note in [Baby G]'s medical notes was a particular dip on 4 June 2015, a desaturation resulting in a drop of blood pressure, [Baby G] was given a saline (fluid) bolus.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the notes made on 8 August 2015, [Baby G]'s summary of problems encountered are as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "'[Baby G] has chronic lung disease, distended tummy, extreme prematurity, damaged kidneys, [Baby G] required numerous blood transfusions.'
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the beginning of August, [Baby G] showed some instability, with temperatures, bradycardia and desaturations. [Baby G] had a routine infection marker which showed she had an infection marker of 84 CRP, which is a raised number. [Baby G] was treated as she had an infection and so was given seven days of antibiotics. [Baby G] was treated for sepsis, [Baby G] was treated for NEC. [Baby G] had high blood sugar during her stay. [Baby G] had a pulmonary haemorrhage on 29 June. This would have been a massive setback.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At that time she had a Broviac line fitted at Alder Hey Hospital. This line was removed on 30 July.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] had a PDA, which is a patent ductus arteriosus, a complication with the heart that was picked up through an echo. [Baby G] had jaundice. [Baby G] had neonatal hypoglycaemia, metabolic bone disease. [Baby G] had low sodium.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the point of transfer of [Baby G] to the Countess of Chester Hospital on 13 August 2015, [Baby G] had to be well enough prior to any transfer. [Baby G]'s condition was as follows. [Baby G] was off the ventilator, then on to CPAP, and at the time of transfer [Baby G] was on high flow oxygen which was a real improvement. From a heart point of view she was stable. Neurology: cranial ultrasound did show a mild bilateral ventricular dilatation, which shows potential bleeding on the brain. Ophthalmology showed no problems. [Baby G]'s haemoglobin level was good.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In respect of her tummy there were no concerns at the point of discharge. [Baby G] had been on full feeds (expressed breast milk) since 22 June. Her discharge feeds were 185ml per kilogram
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: per day via an orogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From a renal point of view, [Baby G]'s kidneys, there were no concerns. [Baby G] required sodium supplements to keep her sodium level up. [Baby G]'s CRP on the day of discharge was shown as normal. Her infection markers were shown as normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G]'s discharge weight was 1,260 grams. I would describe [Baby G]'s condition at the point of transfer to the Countess of Chester Hospital on 13 August 2015 as stable.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G] had her problems at the Countess of Chester, returning to Arrowe Park on 8 September 2015. I did not treat [Baby G] upon her return but I will refer from the medical notes [as read].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby G]'s discharge summary from Arrowe Park Hospital made on 16 September is as follows. [Baby G] had been ventilated for 6 days. However, on discharge she was self-ventilating with no respiratory concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cardiovascularly, there were no concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Neurologically, cranial ultrasound showed that the right side is bigger than the left side and that there are still ventricular patches. Due to [Baby G] having the occasional jittery movements and the results of the cranial ultrasounds, [Baby G] had an MRI scan on her head.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: However, the report had not been received at the time of her discharge.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY
